title: Fibre Property Testing for Raw-Material Quality Control
description: Read article about This article explains fibre property testing for raw-material quality control, covering maturity, fineness, strength, moisture, length, trash, neps, and colour. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Pre-spinning fibre tests support bale choices, blend planning, machine settings, valuation, and forecasts of yarn and fabric performance.
Core checks cover maturity, cross-section, fineness, strength, elongation, uniformity, cohesiveness, moisture regain, length, trash, neps, colour, crimp, and stickiness.
Combined results guide fibre choice and process control.
markdown:
Fibre is the basic raw material for yarn and fabric. Its properties limit spinning performance and influence yarn and fabric quality. Fibre testing is therefore a key part of raw-material quality control.

Fibre testing helps mills select and mix bales, set processing conditions, predict yarn quality and assess cotton for commercial purposes.

This article covers maturity, cross-section, fineness, strength, elongation, uniformity, cohesiveness and moisture regain, followed by other important properties such as length, trash, neps and colour. Examples focus mainly on cotton.

Fibre Maturity

Maturity is the degree of development of the cotton fibre wall. The fibre first grows as a thin tube and then develops a thicker secondary wall as cellulose is deposited. A mature fibre has a thick wall; an immature fibre has a thin wall; a dead fibre has little or no secondary wall. Maturity mainly applies to cotton and other natural cellulosic fibres.

Measures

1. Percentage of mature fibres in a sample.

2. Maturity ratio (M). This expresses maturity as a single value. In the caustic soda method, it is calculated as:

M = (N - D) / 200 + 0.70

Where, N is the percentage of normal (mature) fibres and D is the percentage of dead fibres.

3. Immature fibre content (IFC) is the percentage of immature fibres present in the sample.

Methods of Testing

1.  Caustic soda swelling method. Fibres are treated with about 18 per cent sodium hydroxide and examined under a microscope. Swelling allows fibres to be classified as normal, thin-walled or dead from the wall-thickness/lumen-width relationship.

2. Polarised light method. Fibres are viewed between crossed polarising filters. Differences in interference colours help classify mature and immature fibres.

3. Differential dyeing test. The sample is dyed with red and green dyes. Mature fibres take up more red dye, while immature fibres appear greener, providing a visual indication of maturity.

4. Instrumental methods. Instruments such as AFIS can report maturity ratio and immature fibre content. Micronaire is also influenced by maturity.

Immature fibres are more prone to breakage and nep formation and may produce more waste and yarn breaks. They also absorb dye differently, affecting dyeing quality.

Fibre Cross-Section

Cross-section is the shape and structure of a fibre viewed in a plane perpendicular to its length. Typical cross-sections include:

•   Cotton: bean-shaped or kidney-shaped, with a collapsed central canal called the lumen

•   Wool: roughly circular to oval, with a scaly surface

•   Silk: roughly triangular, with rounded corners

•   Viscose: irregular, with a serrated outline

•   Polyester and Nylon: usually circular, but they can be made in modified shapes, such as trilobal, for special effects

Methods of Testing

5. Microtome sectioning. A bundle of fibres is put in a supporting medium and cut into thin slices. A hand microtome, such as the Hardy microtome, is commonly used. The slices are then viewed under a microscope.

6. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). This gives detailed images of the fibre surface and cross-section.

7. Image analysis. Digital images of cross-sections are analysed by software to measure area, perimeter and wall thickness. These measures can also be used to assess maturity.

Cross-section can affect lustre, handle, stiffness and cover. A trilobal man-made fibre, for example, can reflect light to produce a silk-like sheen. Cross-section also assists fibre identification. Surface features such as wool scales affect handle and friction and should be considered separately from cross-sectional shape.

Fibre Fineness

Fineness describes fibre thickness and is expressed as linear density or diameter.

Measures

8. Linear density. This is expressed in tex, decitex (dtex) or millitex (mtex). Decitex and denier are common for man-made fibres.

9. Diameter. This is expressed in micrometres (µm) and is common for wool.

10.  Micronaire value. This is widely used for cotton and is expressed in micrograms per inch (µg/in). It reflects both fibre fineness and maturity.

Methods of Testing

11.   Airflow method (Micronaire). A fixed-weight cotton sample is compressed in a chamber of fixed volume. Airflow resistance is measured and converted to a micronaire value. A low value may indicate fine fibres, immature fibres, or a combination of both; it should therefore be interpreted with a maturity measure.

12.  Gravimetric method. A bundle of fibres is cut to a known length, the fibres are counted, and the bundle is weighed. Linear density is then calculated from weight and total length.

13.  Microscopic method. Fibre diameters are measured under a microscope, usually a projection microscope. This is a standard reference method for wool.

14.  Vibroscope method. A single fibre is held under tension and made to vibrate. Its linear density is calculated from its natural vibration frequency. This method is used for man-made fibres.

15.  Optical instruments. Laser and image-based systems measure wool fibre diameter quickly on large numbers of fibres.

Finer fibres allow more fibres in a given yarn cross-section, supporting finer yarn counts and, within suitable limits, better strength and evenness. They can also give a softer handle. Fineness is therefore an important factor in determining spinning limits.

Fibre Strength

Fibre strength is the force required to break a fibre or fibre bundle.

Measures

16.  Breaking force. This is measured in centinewtons (cN) or grams-force.

17.  Tenacity is breaking force divided by linear density. It is expressed in g/tex or cN/tex and allows fibres of different fineness to be compared.

18.  Pressley Index. This is the breaking load of a fibre bundle in pounds divided by its weight in milligrams.

Methods of Testing

1. Bundle testing. Cotton fibres are usually tested as flat bundles, because single cotton fibres are short and variable.

•   The Pressley tester breaks a bundle at zero gauge length, with the jaws touching.

•   The Stelometer breaks a bundle at 1/8-inch (3.2 mm) gauge length. It also records elongation.

•   The High Volume Instrument (HVI) tests bundles automatically at 1/8-inch gauge. It reports strength in g/tex.

2. Single fibre testing. Man-made fibres and long natural fibres can be tested one at a time on tensile testers that work on the constant rate of extension principle.

Gauge Length

Gauge length affects the measured strength. At zero gauge length, weak sections have less influence; at a 1/8-inch gauge length, a longer portion of the fibre is subjected to the test. Gauge length should therefore be stated when comparing results.

Fibre strength contributes to yarn strength and influences processing performance, including permissible processing speeds and end-break frequency.

Fibre Elongation

Elongation is the percentage increase in fibre length at break relative to its original length.

Elongation (per cent) = (extension at break / initial length) × 100

Methods of Testing

19.  Elongation is recorded during strength testing using instruments such as the Stelometer, HVI or a single-fibre tensile tester.

20. The load–elongation curve also gives the work of rupture, which reflects the toughness of the fibre.

Natural cellulosic fibres, such as cotton and linen, have low elongation. Wool and many man-made fibres, such as nylon and polyester, have much higher elongation.

Adequate elongation allows fibres to absorb sudden loads during processing with less breakage. It also contributes to yarn elongation and fabric durability.

Fibre Uniformity

In fibre testing, uniformity usually refers to the distribution of fibre lengths within a sample. Uniformity can also describe consistency in properties such as fineness or maturity.

21.  Upper Half Mean Length (UHML): mean length of the longer half of fibres by weight; it is related to staple length.

22. Mean Length (ML). This is the average length of all the fibres.

23. 2.5 per cent span length: length exceeded by 2.5 per cent of fibres in a fibrogram; commonly used as a measure of effective length.

24. 50 per cent span length: length exceeded by 50 per cent of fibres in the same test.

Measures of Uniformity

1. Uniformity Index (UI). This is reported by HVI.

UI = (ML / UHML) × 100

2. Uniformity Ratio (UR). This is reported by the fibrograph.

UR = (50 per cent span length / 2.5 per cent span length) × 100

3. Short Fibre Content (SFC). This is the percentage of fibres shorter than 12.7 mm (0.5 inch).

Higher UI or UR and lower SFC indicate greater length uniformity.

Methods of Testing

25. Length and uniformity are measured with the fibrograph, HVI and AFIS.

26. Older reference methods, such as the Baer sorter and comb sorter, arrange fibres by length to produce a length distribution diagram.

Uniform fibres draft more smoothly and contribute to even yarn. High short-fibre content can increase thick and thin places, hairiness, fly and waste.

Fibre Cohesiveness

Cohesiveness is the ability of fibres to cling together during processing. It helps maintain the fibre web, sliver and roving before twist is added. Cohesion is influenced by fibre surface, shape and crimp:

•   Cotton: natural convolutions (twists along the fibre)

•   Wool: surface scales and natural crimp

•   Man-Made Fibres: crimp added during manufacture, and spin finish, which controls fibre-to-fibre friction

Methods of Testing

27. Fibre-to-fibre friction test. A fibre or group of fibres is pulled against another and the frictional force is measured. The coefficient of friction is calculated from the result.

28. Sliver cohesion test. A sliver or roving is drafted between roller pairs, and the force required for drafting is measured as drafting or cohesive force.

29. Crimp measurement. For man-made fibres, the number of crimps per unit length and crimp percentage are measured, since crimp strongly affects cohesion.

Too little cohesion can cause web or sliver breakage and fibre fly. Excessive cohesion can hinder drafting and produce uneven sliver. A suitable balance is needed for smooth processing.

Moisture Regain

Moisture regain is the weight of water expressed as a percentage of oven-dry weight. Moisture content expresses water as a percentage of the total sample weight.

Formulas

Moisture Regain (per cent) = (W - D) / D × 100

Moisture Content (per cent) = (W - D) / W × 100

Where, W is the weight of the sample and D is its oven-dry weight.

Moisture regain depends on the surrounding atmosphere, so fibres are conditioned and tested under specified conditions. A common standard atmosphere is 20 °C and 65 per cent relative humidity; some tropical testing conditions use 27 °C.

Different fibres absorb different amounts of moisture. The values below are approximate, at standard conditions:

| Fibre | Approximate moisture regain (%) |
| Cotton | 8.5 |
| Viscose | 13 |
| Wool | 16 |
| Silk | 11 |
| Nylon | 4 |
| Acrylic | 1.5 |
| Polyester | 0.4 |

Commercial regain values vary with fibre form and applicable standards; the relevant standard should be checked before using them for trade calculations.

Methods of Testing

30. Oven-Drying Method. A sample is weighed, dried at about 105–110 °C until its weight is constant, and weighed again. This is the reference method.

31.  Electrical Methods. Moisture meters measure electrical resistance or capacitance, which changes with moisture. They give quick readings on bales and packages.

32. Infrared Methods. These measure the absorption of infrared radiation by water in the sample.

Because fibres are bought and sold by weight, moisture affects commercial weight. Invoice weight may be based on a specified commercial regain:

Commercial weight = Oven-dry weight × (100 + commercial regain) / 100

Moisture regain affects:

•   Trade: moisture affects the weight used for commercial transactions.

•   Processing: very dry fibres can build static charge, while very damp fibres may stick and cause lapping.

•   Strength: cotton generally becomes stronger when wet, while viscose generally becomes weaker.

•   Comfort: fibres with higher moisture regain can absorb more moisture from the body and may improve wearer comfort.

•   Dimensions: moisture absorption causes fibre swelling and can influence fabric dimensional behaviour.

Other Important Properties

The eight properties above do not give a complete picture of fibre quality. Other routinely tested properties include length, trash, neps, colour, crimp and stickiness.

1. Fibre Length

Fibre length is a major determinant of spinning performance. It affects the count range, yarn strength, evenness and hairiness. Longer fibres generally provide better fibre control and can contribute to stronger, smoother yarns. Length is expressed as staple length, UHML, mean length or span length and measured by methods such as hand stapling, Baer sorter, fibrograph, HVI and AFIS. Drafting settings are selected according to fibre length.

2. Trash Content

Trash is non-fibrous matter in cotton, such as leaf, seed-coat fragments, stalk and dust. The Shirley Trash Analyser measures trash percentage by weight, while HVI estimates trash from camera images. High trash increases waste and can contribute to machinery, yarn and fabric faults.

3. Neps

Neps are small knots of tangled fibres. They can form from immature fibres during ginning and processing. AFIS reports nep count per gram; nep boards can also be used for assessment. Neps may appear as visible specks in yarn and fabric, especially after dyeing.

4. Colour

Cotton colour is measured by HVI using a colour-measuring system. Reflectance (Rd) indicates brightness and yellowness (+b) is used with Rd to determine colour grade. Colour affects cotton value and dyeing or bleaching behaviour.

5. Crimp

Crimp is the waviness of a fibre. It is important for wool and man-made staple fibres and is measured as crimps per unit length or crimp percentage. Crimp affects cohesion, bulk, warmth and handle.

6. Stickiness

Some cotton is sticky because of sugars from insects (honeydew) or the plant. Instrumental tests assess sticky points by heating or pressing the fibre. Sticky cotton can adhere to rollers and card clothing and interrupt production.

Properties Specific to Man-Made Fibres

Man-made fibres may also be tested for heat shrinkage and spin-finish content. Heat shrinkage affects dimensional stability during dyeing and finishing, while spin finish influences fibre friction and static during processing.

| Property | Main measure | Main methods or instruments |
| Maturity | Maturity ratio, % mature fibres, IFC | Caustic soda test, polarised light, differential dyeing, AFIS |
| Cross-section | Shape, area, wall thickness | Microtome, microscope, SEM, image analysis |
| Fineness | Micronaire, tex, dtex, µm | Airflow (Micronaire), gravimetric, microscope, vibroscope |
| Strength | g/tex, Pressley Index | Pressley, Stelometer, HVI, single fibre tester |
| Elongation | % at break | Stelometer, HVI, single fibre tester |
| Uniformity | UI, UR, SFC | Fibrograph, HVI, AFIS, Baer sorter |
| Cohesiveness | Friction, drafting force, crimp | Fibre friction test, sliver cohesion test |
| Moisture regain | % regain, % content | Oven-drying, moisture meter, infrared |
| Length | UHML, ML, 2.5% span length | Hand stapling, Baer sorter, fibrograph, HVI, AFIS |
| Trash | % by weight | Shirley Trash Analyser, HVI |
| Neps | Count per gram | AFIS, nep board |
| Colour | Rd, +b, colour grade | HVI colorimeter |

Fibre properties are interrelated. Micronaire reflects both fineness and maturity, so the two should be interpreted together. Immature fibres can contribute to weakness and neps. Fineness and length influence the practical spinning limit; short-fibre content affects yarn evenness and hairiness; moisture affects strength, static and processing behaviour.

No single test is sufficient to assess fibre quality. Mills therefore consider the combined results when selecting and mixing fibres and controlling processing conditions.

Fibre testing assesses raw-material properties before processing. Combined results for structure, fineness, length, strength, uniformity, moisture and other quality characteristics help mills select and mix fibres, set processing conditions and maintain consistent yarn quality.
author: Dr Lipsa Mohapatra
